tldr: A motion-tracking policy for a humanoid trained via reinforcement learning sees its survival rate plunge to 15% with just a 40 ms command delay. This paper shows that simply randomizing the delay (0–50 ms) during training widens the delay margin significantly to 50–70 ms.
overview:
Reinforcement learning for humanoid motion tracking (mimicking human movement) has achieved impressive results, even on real hardware. Typically, policies are trained in a GPU simulator with dynamics randomization and checked in a second simulator (a sim-to-sim check) before going anywhere near physical hardware. However, real robot control loops inevitably suffer from latency—the time between when a policy issues a command and when the actuator responds. While classical control treats delay as a critical factor that undermines stability, how much delay a learned humanoid controller can actually tolerate, and how training-time delay randomization truly helps, had not been quantitatively investigated.

The authors thoroughly evaluated robustness to command delay using a 24-joint humanoid tracking five motions extracted from monocular video. They built an independent CPU MuJoCo evaluation harness separate from the training environment (mjlab), rigorously verified its physical model match against the training setup, and evaluated policy survival rates under delays introduced in 10 ms increments.

The experiments revealed a steep cliff: policies trained without delay randomization tolerated only 20–30 ms of delay, with survival dropping sharply from 67% to 15% when delay reached 40 ms. In contrast, randomizing delay between 0 and 50 ms during training pushed the delay margin out to 50–70 ms and maintained a 95% survival rate at 40 ms. By comparing this against a control arm trained for the same number of extra iterations without delay, the authors proved that the gain comes from the delay randomization itself rather than longer training, and they confirmed the exact same phenomenon holds for a policy trained in PhysX.
contributions: Built an independent CPU MuJoCo evaluation harness strictly matched to the training setup, identifying that initial sim-to-sim discrepancies stemmed from a missing floor and a mismatched timestep rather than the physics engines themselves.

Measured the command delay (delay margin) that an RL-based humanoid motion tracker can tolerate in 10 ms increments, quantitatively exposing a sharp drop in survival at 20–30 ms when delay is unaddressed.

Demonstrated that adding 0–50 ms delay randomization during training widens the delay margin to 50–70 ms, verified against an equally trained control arm to isolate the effect of randomization from extra training time.

Showed that a policy trained in Isaac Lab (PhysX) exhibits the same vulnerability to delay and identical gains from randomization, confirming the findings do not depend on a specific training framework.

sections.heading: Why measure a humanoid's robustness to delay?
sections.summary: RL-based motion-tracking policies can pull off challenging behaviors on real robots, but their robustness to actuator command delay has not been adequately measured. This study rigorously evaluates the delay margin of a 24-joint humanoid using an independent validation simulator.
sections.details:
Advances in reinforcement learning for motion tracking have enabled humanoids to reproduce highly dynamic movements. Standard practice involves training with domain randomization (deliberately perturbing environmental parameters) in a GPU simulator, followed by a sanity check in a second simulator (a sim-to-sim verification) before deploying to hardware.

Yet real control loops always suffer from latency—the interval between when a policy outputs an action and when the actuators physically respond. In classical control theory, delay is a primary hazard that erodes phase margin and destabilizes systems. In humanoid RL, however, the common approach has simply been to toss in a small random delay of around 0–20 ms during training, leaving it unclear how much delay policies can actually withstand and what that randomization genuinely improves.

This paper evaluates the delay margin—how much delay a policy can tolerate—on a 24-joint humanoid tracking five motions captured from monocular video. Testing mjlab-trained policies in an independent CPU MuJoCo harness, the authors deliver three core contributions: verifying the evaluation harness, quantitatively measuring delay margins, and strictly isolating the effect of delay randomization from extra training time.

sections.heading: Delay modeling in RL and the lineage of sim-to-sim checks
sections.summary: While delay simulation and actuator system identification for sim-to-real transfer have been studied before, systematic measurement of delay tolerance in motion trackers was missing. This work examines the effective delay margin of a learned nonlinear closed-loop system.
sections.details:
### Handling delay in reinforcement learning
Simulating communication and actuator delays for sim-to-real transfer dates back to early quadruped locomotion research. Recent efforts have also focused on identifying actuator dynamics and latencies directly from real-world data. In modern humanoid locomotion frameworks, randomizing actuation delay up to around 20 ms during training has become common. Theoretical RL has also analyzed Markov decision processes with delay, but the measurements here adopt a control engineering perspective to evaluate the empirical delay margin of a learned, nonlinear feedback system.

### Motion tracking and sim-to-sim checks
Tracking motions extracted from human video has progressed rapidly, achieving acrobatic skills on physical hardware. Alongside this, validating policies across different simulators (sim-to-sim) has become a standard step in frameworks like Humanoid-Gym, joined by multi-simulator co-training in PolySim and real-data residual compensation in ASAP. Still, prior work left an open question: how does training-time delay randomization actually change a motion tracker's tolerance to delay? That is the exact question this study tackles.

sections.heading: Behind the scenes: Robot, motions, delay model, and a verified test harness
sections.summary: A 24-joint, 28.9 kg humanoid is trained with PPO on five video-extracted motions. Policies exported to ONNX are evaluated in a CPU MuJoCo harness that faithfully reproduces the training model's physical parameters.
sections.details:
### Robot and controller
The target robot is a humanoid with 24 actuators (6 per leg, 2 at the waist, 5 per arm) weighing 28.9 kg. Each joint is driven by a 200 Hz (5 ms step) PD control loop subject to manufacturer torque limits. The high-level policy runs at 50 Hz (20 ms period) and outputs target joint position offsets relative to a default standing pose. The 135-dimensional observation space includes target joint positions and velocities, torso position and orientation relative to the reference, base linear and angular velocities, current joint positions and velocities, and the previous action. Policies are trained using PPO across 4,096 parallel environments on a GPU.

### Delay model and training schedule
When delay randomization is enabled, target joint position commands receive an integer-step delay $L \sim \mathcal{U}\{0, \dots, 10\}$ (0–50 ms). This delay value is resampled every 200 steps (1 s) per robot. In the experiments, a base policy is first trained without delay for 3,000 iterations (12,998 iterations for tennis serve). From that checkpoint, training branches into two arms for another 3,000 iterations: a control arm trained without delay, and a delay arm trained with delay randomization, each across three random seeds. This clean split confirms that performance gains stem from delay randomization itself rather than simply training longer.

### Reference motions and evaluation harness
Five reference motions were extracted from monocular video using GVHMR and GMR (a tennis serve, three dance routines, and shadow boxing), spanning durations from 8.7 to 26.4 seconds. Trained policies are exported to ONNX and evaluated in pure CPU MuJoCo. The evaluation harness faithfully reproduces the floor, contact parameters, 5 ms timestep, and solver settings. An episode fails if excessive posture degradation occurs (torso or end-effector positions/orientations deviate by more than 0.25 m). Stress tests are conducted by applying constant command delays (0–80 ms in 10 ms increments) and external perturbations.

sections.heading: Experimental findings: From harness sanity checks to dramatic margin gains
sections.summary: After tracing early harness discrepancies to a missing floor and a timestep mismatch, delay tolerance was evaluated. Delay randomization broadened the margin from 20–30 ms to 50–70 ms, driving survival at 40 ms delay from 15% up to 95%.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Verifying the evaluation harness
When the tennis policy was run on an early version of the harness, tracking error exploded to 4.6–8.9 rad, completely diverging (compared to 0.78 rad during training). Ablation tests isolated the issue: it was not a difference between physics engines, but simply that the robot description file lacked a floor plane and the harness used a 2 ms timestep instead of the 5 ms training timestep. Once aligned with the training environment, the harness reproduced tracking performance identical to training.

### 4.2 How delay randomization expands the delay margin
The delay margin is defined as the maximum delay at which at least half of the episodes complete successfully. For the unrandomized control arm, this margin was only 30 ms for four motions and 20 ms for the studio dance. Survival fell off a cliff as delay grew by just 10 ms: from an average of 67% at 30 ms down to 15% at 40 ms, 1% at 50 ms, and 0% at 60 ms. In sharp contrast, the group trained with 0–50 ms delay randomization saw its delay margin stretch to 50–70 ms. At a 40 ms delay, survival averaged 95% (75–100%), exhibiting a graceful degradation rather than a sudden catastrophic failure.

### 4.3 Gains come from delay randomization, not extra training
Comparing the base policy (before branching) with the control arm showed that additional delay-free training yielded almost no improvement: control policies survived only 0–9 out of 20 runs at 40 ms delay, barely different from the base policy (0–2 runs). In contrast, all delay-randomized policies survived 15 or more runs. This proves the dramatic boost in survival is directly caused by the delay randomization intervention, not simply by training for more iterations.

### 4.4 Robustness to other perturbations and trade-offs
The price of delay randomization was a slight increase in nominal (zero-delay) joint tracking error by 0.02–0.06 rad across four motions. Under reduced ground friction (0.15), robustness actually improved—doubling tennis survival from 23% to 48%. However, on the most dynamic studio dance, tolerance to a 2 kg payload, external pushes, and missing base velocity observations dropped noticeably. For highly dynamic motions, dedicating control capacity to withstand delay appears to leave less headroom to absorb other external disturbances.

### 4.5 Validation with an alternate physics engine (PhysX)
Evaluating a policy trained in Isaac Lab (PhysX engine) within the same MuJoCo harness revealed the exact same trend. The model trained without delay had a 0% survival rate (0/20) at 40 ms delay, whereas the model trained with 0–50 ms delay randomization survived 15/20 runs. This confirms the vulnerability and its solution are not quirks of any single simulator.

sections.heading: Why standard sim-to-sim checks miss delay fragility
sections.summary: Standard zero-delay sim-to-sim checks pass every policy, masking their vulnerability to latency. Because the common 0–20 ms randomization range falls entirely within an unrandomized tracker's built-in margin, training should randomize across a wider range guided by measured hardware latency.
sections.details:
Under a standard synchronous sim-to-sim check, every policy in this study passed cleanly. Nearly all episodes succeed when delay is between 0 and 10 ms. Failures emerge only when delay is introduced, and because collapse can happen abruptly over a mere 10 ms window, checking only a single delay value risks missing the cliff entirely.

The 0–20 ms delay randomization commonly used in humanoid locomotion training actually sits entirely inside the margin that an unrandomized policy naturally possesses (20–30 ms). The substantial gains in this work came from randomizing beyond that inherent margin, up to 50 ms. For real-world deployment, engineers should measure the actual latency from policy output to actuator response on the physical robot and configure training randomization to comfortably exceed that value.

For moderate motions, the cost is modest—tracking error increases by only 0.02–0.06 rad. But for aggressive motions pushed near physical limits, engineers must account for the trade-off with other perturbation margins. Finally, because measuring delay margin requires nothing more than placing a delay buffer in the evaluation harness, the authors argue it should be reported as a standard sim-to-sim benchmark metric.

sections.heading: Measuring delay tolerance to build real confidence before hardware deployment
sections.summary: This study systematically measured the delay margin of learned motion trackers, proving that training-time delay randomization pushes margins out to 50–70 ms. Next steps include measuring latency on physical hardware and testing how accurately simulated delay margins predict real-world stability.
sections.details:
Using a carefully verified independent simulator, this research systematically measured the command delay humanoid motion-tracking policies can withstand. Without explicit delay mitigation, policies tolerate only 20–30 ms of delay before survival plummets at 40 ms. Randomizing delay over 0–50 ms during training reliably expands this margin to 50–70 ms, an effect that extra training alone cannot produce.

While limitations remain—such as trade-offs with other disturbance margins during highly dynamic motions and assuming ideal PD actuators—these findings provide actionable guidelines for real-world deployment. Future work should measure actual command latencies on physical humanoid hardware and verify how well delay margins measured in simulation predict stability in the real world.

takeaways: Tracking policies trained without delay mitigation hit their tolerance limit at 20–30 ms of delay, collapsing abruptly with just an additional 10 ms of latency.

The 0–20 ms delay randomization common in locomotion training falls inside the margin an unrandomized policy already has; real margin gains (50–70 ms) require randomizing beyond that intrinsic threshold (e.g., 0–50 ms).
Discrepancies in sim-to-sim verification often stem from basic environment misconfigurations—such as a missing floor or mismatched physics timesteps—rather than differences between physics engines.
Widening delay tolerance comes with trade-offs: highly dynamic motions exhibit slightly looser tracking precision and reduced robustness to other disturbances such as pushes or payload additions.
limitations: All experiments were conducted purely in simulation with ideal torque-limited PD actuators; neither actuator latency nor physical tracking was validated on hardware.
While the delay value was resampled every second during training, the evaluation harness held delay constant throughout each episode, presenting a somewhat harsher test condition.

The study did not explore mitigation strategies, such as curriculum learning or feeding delay values into the observation space, to alleviate the loss of disturbance robustness seen during dynamic motions.
